comment.value: The paper presents NoRA, a new reasoning benchmark designed to test neural relational reasoning in a systematic way. The benchmark is thoughtfully designed to incorporate increased complexity across multiple dimensions, including ambiguity in facts, multi-relation entity pairs, and non-path-based reasoning patterns. In addition, the authors propose difficulty metrics, including reasoning depth and backtrack load, and systematically evaluate a range of existing models. The results reveal that current methods perform poorly under these more challenging conditions, underscoring the need for more robust approaches. All reviewers agree that this is an important and timely contribution to the field, and I fully agree.
I would like to thank the authors for the rebuttal. My concerns are fully addressed.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the careful reading of the paper and supportive feedback.

# W1

> All stories share one family-style ontology and generalization to other domains is untested. Providing at least one additional rule-set to demonstrate portability of the generation pipeline would be helpful.

Thanks for this suggestion. We have started working on a second set of world rules, called Hetionet, and will add the corresponding experimental results to the paper.
In the Hetionet world, there are three kinds of entities: compounds, diseases, and genes. Compounds and genes can palliate a disease. Compounds can be used to treat a disease, or they can be marked as unusable for treating a disease. Off-path reasoning emerges because, to be used to treat a disease, a compound must both palliate that disease and have no side effects. Compounds and genes can also upregulate a gene; if an entity upregulates a gene that palliates a disease, then the entity itself palliates that disease. Compounds can be similar to each other in three different ways:

* ss2(c1, c2) means c1 and c2 palliate the same diseases;
* ss3(c1, c2) means c1 and c2 either both have side effects or neither has side effects;
* ss1(c1, c2) means they have the same regulatory properties towards genes.

Hetionet has significantly different regularity than the NoRA world, particularly because there is no hierarchical tree-like structure—two compounds can be related in multiple ways concurrently (in NoRA, your uncle cannot be your brother). We created training sets, test-D, and test-OPEC-na in a similar way to NoRA. Crucially, as for NoRA, all examples observed during testing are stitched-up versions of one or more examples seen during training. The results are shown below. 

 Model            | test-in-distribution (EM) | test-OPEC-na (EM)   | test-D (EM) |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|-----------------|----------------|
| Multi-edge ET  | 0.75    | 0.54          | 0.87         |

This drop-off for higher OPEC examples is due to the multi-edge Edge Transformer’s inability to perform systematic reasoning since all examples it sees during testing are joined versions of examples it has seen during training.

# W2

> Since BL is defined as the maximum number of simultaneous partial bindings the prover must keep alive while exploring a proof tree, in practice it is highly dependent on how individual rules are written. For example, splitting a 3-body rule into two shorter rules may reduces BL from 3 to 1 without changing the underlying reasoning difficulty. A similar drift is observed for OPEC when optional edges are inlined into rules. Consequently, BL/OPEC values cannot be compared across domains unless the rule factorization scheme is fixed.

We use these difficulty metrics to construct test sets that assess systematic generalization (by selecting test examples that are strictly harder, according to one of the metrics, than the training examples). For this specific purpose, it doesn’t matter that the metrics are dependent on how the rules were encoded. All that matters is that they guarantee that the test examples are fundamentally different, in some way, from the training examples. This indeed means that care would be needed when comparing BL values across different domains, but it’s not clear to us that this is really something we would want to do. 

Note that OPEC is independent of how the rules are encoded, so comparing OPEC values across domains should be more meaningful.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the careful reading of the paper and supportive feedback.

# W1

> Metrics like reasoning depth and backtrack load depend on rule implementation (§6). E.g., alternate rule formulations could reduce depth, skewing difficulty assessments.

The primary reason why we need these difficulty metrics is to construct test sets that assess systematic generalization (by selecting test examples that are strictly harder, according to one of the metrics, than the training examples). For this specific purpose, it doesn’t matter that the metrics are dependent on how the rules were encoded. All that matters is that they guarantee that the test examples are fundamentally different, in some way, from the training examples.

Note that we also consider OPEC, as a variant of BL which does not depend on the rule formulations. The empirical results we obtained with the test sets based on OPEC and BL are in close alignment. Regarding reasoning depth, since this is a commonly used and intuitive metric, we believe it is useful to include this metric, even though it indeed depends on how the rules are encoded.

The world rules in NoRA have been carefully constructed to be minimal (i.e. we don’t include rules that can be derived from the other rules), which also helps to ensure that the reasoning depth and BL values are meaningful.

# W2

> Key elements are only addressed in supplements (e.g., world rules, ambiguity sampling).

The supplementary materials contain additional technical details, we believe this is in line with standard practice.

# F1

> How do BL/OPEC correlate?

BL and OPEC were both designed to measure how much off-path reasoning is needed to solve an example in the NoRA dataset. BL is capable of capturing more general types of back-and-forth reasoning than OPEC. However, unlike OPEC, BL depends on the particular way the rule set is constructed (as the reviewer has pointed out). We therefore introduce both in this study. 

BL and OPEC can be controlled independently, hence the correlation depends on how the dataset was sampled. For the dataset with ambiguity, we observe a Pearson correlation coefficient between OPEC and BL of 0.321 (95% confidence interval via bootstrap: [0.3086, 0.3359]). For the dataset without ambiguity, we observe a Pearson correlation coefficient between OPEC and BL of 0.4650 (95% confidence interval via bootstrap: [0.4503, 0.4840]). We will add a scatterplot to the paper to illustrate this.

# F2

> Please consider testing rule induction without explicit rule provision.

Note that for our main experiments, the rules are not provided, and models are required to learn the rules from the training examples.

Only in  the experiments with o3 and o4-mini, we have directly provided the  world rules to the models, as our aim was to show that these models also struggle with off-path reasoning, even when they are not required to learn the rules. Learning rules with LLMs/LRMs is an interesting topic, but we believe that exploring this would be outside the scope of our paper. Moreover, if these models are not able to reason with the considered rules, it seems unlikely that they would be capable of learning the rules (at least not when uninformative predicate names are used; the models have demonstrated that they are aware of most of the NoRA rules from their experiences in the real world).

We thank the reviewer for the careful reading of the paper and supportive feedback.

# W1

> One possible weakness is that the paper doesn't evaluate models from a counterfactual reasoning perspective. For example, it would be interesting to see whether models update their predictions logically when a single input fact is modified — say, replacing “a is father_of b” with “a is mother_of b.” This kind of test would help reveal whether the models are truly learning the underlying rules or just overfitting to distributional patterns.

The main motivation behind systematic generalization tests, where the test instances are strictly harder than the training examples along some dimension of difficulty, is to test whether the models are “genuinely reasoning” rather than relying on shortcuts, i.e., overfitting to distributional patterns. This is why, in each of our test sets, we ensure that the problems are harder than the training examples in some way (and thus out of distribution). 

Designing a true counterfactual test would be challenging for our setting. For instance, after replacing “father of” by “mother of”, the model would likely still rely on shortcuts (since it may have seen versions of both the “father of” and “mother of” versions during training).

However, to analyze more explicitly whether the models have learned the rules, we will add an analysis where the test graph consists precisely of the body of a rule, and we verify whether the prediction matches the head of the rule. This will provide insights into whether there are some rules which the model has failed to learn.

# W2

> Minor: Line 122 looks grammatically weird, although I can get it.

Thanks for the suggestion, we will rephrase this.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the careful reading of the paper and their helpful feedback. 

The critical comments from the reviewer primarily relate to the fact that the reasoning problems we consider can, in theory, be captured by current GNNs and transformer based models. However, when it comes to reasoning with GNNs, we would like to contrast two fundamentally different lines of work:

1. There is work on increasing the theoretical expressivity of GNNs, often aimed at targeting higher-order versions of the Weisfeiler-Leman test by incorporating higher-order interactions. This is also important, but it is *not* the focus of our paper.

2. There is work on addressing the fact that standard GNNs (and transformers) struggle in tasks that require systematic generalization. The focus here is not on what forms of reasoning the models can capture in theory, but on how they generalize in practice.

The work on CLUTRR already showed that standard GNNs and transformers fail at very simple systematic generalization tasks. Crucially, this is the case for models which are theoretically capable of carrying out the kind of reasoning that is needed for CLUTRR. However, in practice, the models learn shortcuts rather than genuinely learning to reason, which makes them fail on out-of-distribution test examples.

In response, the community has developed models with stronger inductive biases (e.g. CTP, NCRL, EpiGNN). These models perform well on benchmarks such as CLUTRR, by imposing strong inductive biases. Unfortunately, these biases constrain the model to focus only on path-based reasoning. In our paper, we highlight the fact that path-based reasoning is often not enough for real-world problems, and we propose a benchmark to support the development of the next generation of models.

# W1

> The core claim—that existing models fundamentally rely on path-based reasoning and cannot handle off-path or multi-path inference—is not well justified. Modern graph-based and neuro-symbolic methods (e.g., GNNs with multi-hop message passing, neural logic machines, EpiGNNs) can, in principle, capture these forms of reasoning.

There are indeed many models that can, in theory, carry out off-path reasoning, but these models tend to perform poorly in settings that require systematic generalization (Bergen et. al. 2021, Sinha et. al. 2019). Models that have been designed for systematic generalization, such as CTP, NCRL, EpiGNN, only carry out path-based reasoning. Edge Transformers occupy a kind of middle ground: their inductive bias is weaker, which allows them to do off-path reasoning, but the weaker inductive bias limits their potential for systematic generalization (as seen in path-based benchmarks such as CLUTRR). This is also confirmed by our experiments: while edge transformers perform best of all the models tested, they still perform extremely poorly in settings that require off-path reasoning. This shows that our benchmark is highly challenging for existing models.

# W2

> While NoRA introduces new metrics and difficulty settings, the underlying reasoning task is still binary relation prediction between two entities. The work does not move toward more expressive or realistic reasoning formats such as higher-order interactions, ternary predicates, or subgraph-level reasoning.

Our central motivation was to find the simplest forms of reasoning for which current models fail. As the results in our paper show, we do not have to go beyond predicting binary relations, and we do not have to go beyond reasoning about Horn rules, to “break” the current models. 

Higher-order interactions, ternary predicates and subgraph-level reasoning are relevant in works that study the theoretical expressivity of GNNs, but we believe that they are less relevant in the context of learning to reason and systematic generalization, since the current models are not even capable of tackling much simpler forms of reasoning, which is something that needs to be addressed before (much) more challenging settings can be considered. 

# W3

> The paper criticizes path-based inductive bias, but the proposed benchmark still operates within the same basic relational framework. The “off-path” examples, while harder, do not require a fundamentally new class of models and can be addressed with existing architectures with appropriate training.

The point is that current models with current training strategies fail on the proposed benchmark, and addressing this is far from trivial. Whether the benchmark can be solved with current models using innovative training strategies, or whether it will require introducing novel models, is something that will need to be seen in future work. But either way, the benchmark targets a challenging problem that is currently out of reach.

# W4

> The work designs harder data but does not propose new modeling techniques or theoretical insights. It reveals limitations in existing models under this new setup, but does not offer algorithmic progress to address them.

This is correct, but we believe this is appropriate for the Datasets and Benchmarks track.

summary.value: This paper introduces NoRA, a new benchmark aimed at testing systematic neural relational reasoning beyond the commonly assumed “path-based reasoning” paradigm. The benchmark is designed with increased complexity along several dimensions, including ambiguity in facts, multi-relation pairs, and non-path reasoning patterns. The authors also propose difficulty metrics (e.g., reasoning depth, backtrack load, OPEC) and evaluate a range of existing models on the benchmark, showing that current methods perform poorly under these settings.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper addresses an important question in neural reasoning: how to assess and encourage models that generalize beyond path-like inference patterns.

- The diagnostic metrics such as OPEC and backtrack load provide useful tools for evaluating the complexity of reasoning beyond traditional path-following.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The core claim—that existing models fundamentally rely on path-based reasoning and cannot handle off-path or multi-path inference—is not well justified. Modern graph-based and neuro-symbolic methods (e.g., GNNs with multi-hop message passing, neural logic machines, EpiGNNs) can, in principle, capture these forms of reasoning.

- While NoRA introduces new metrics and difficulty settings, the underlying reasoning task is still binary relation prediction between two entities. The work does not move toward more expressive or realistic reasoning formats such as higher-order interactions, ternary predicates, or subgraph-level reasoning.

- The paper criticizes path-based inductive bias, but the proposed benchmark still operates within the same basic relational framework. The “off-path” examples, while harder, do not require a fundamentally new class of models and can be addressed with existing architectures with appropriate training.

- The work designs harder data but does not propose new modeling techniques or theoretical insights. It reveals limitations in existing models under this new setup, but does not offer algorithmic progress to address them.

summary.value: The paper considers the problem of systematic neural relational reasoning, which involves predicting relationships between entities by learning and applying logical rules in a way that compositionally generalizes to novel scenarios. To address the limitations of existing benchmarks that primarily focus on path-based reasoning, the paper introduces NoRA (Non-Path Reasoning with Ambiguous Facts), a new benchmark that challenges models with more realistic and diverse reasoning tasks. A key novelty of the benchmark is that it includes the tasks that require off-path reasoning. The authors also propose new evaluation metrics to assess problem instances, and use these metrics to create several dataset splits. The performance of existing methods is then evaluated on these splits.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper is overall well-written. The main idea is clear, and the structure is easy to follow. 

- Systematic neural relational reasoning is an important research direction, and the paper makes a meaningful contribution by constructing a more realistic dataset for evaluating such tasks. The motivation is sound, and the proposed benchmark aligns well with the challenges faced in real-world reasoning.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- One possible weakness is that the paper doesn't evaluate models from a counterfactual reasoning perspective. For example, it would be interesting to see whether models update their predictions logically when a single input fact is modified — say, replacing “a is father_of b” with “a is mother_of b.” This kind of test would help reveal whether the models are truly learning the underlying rules or just overfitting to distributional patterns.

- Minor: Line 122 looks grammatically weird, although I can get it.

summary.value:
The paper introduces NoRA (Non-Path Reasoning with Ambiguous Facts), a benchmark for evaluating systematic relational reasoning in neural models. It addresses limitations in existing benchmarks (e.g., CLUTRR, STaR), which primarily test path-based reasoning (composing relations along a single path between entities). 

NoRA adds three key challenges:

1. Off-path reasoning: Requires detours through entities not on direct paths (e.g., Figure 1).

2. Ambiguous facts: Entities may have uncertain relationships (e.g., "A is father of B or C"), resolved via constraint-based reasoning.

3. Multi-relational entities: Entities can simultaneously hold hierarchical/independent relationships (e.g., "Ann is both aunt and maternal aunt of Todd").

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Existing benchmarks (CLUTRR, STaR) overemphasize path-based reasoning, enabling model shortcuts (§1–2). NoRA forces non-compositional reasoning (e.g., OPEC >0), better reflecting real-world complexity.
2. Clearly contrasts with CLUTRR (path-based, no ambiguity) and STaR (multi-path but still path-centric) (§1, §2). Justifies need for ambiguity and off-path reasoning.
3. Well-structured logical flow from problem statement to experiments. Figures effectively illustrate non-path reasoning.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Metrics like reasoning depth and backtrack load depend on rule implementation (§6). E.g., alternate rule formulations could reduce depth, skewing difficulty assessments.
2. Key elements are only addressed in supplements (e.g., world rules, ambiguity sampling).

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset is hosted on Hugging Face with Croissant metadata. About the reproducibility, data generation via Clingo (MIT-licensed) is documented (§3, §12) and training/test splits clearly defined (Table 1). Maybe it would be better to add a statement about the license of the dataset.

additional_feedback.value:
1. How do BL/OPEC correlate?
2. Please considering testing rule induction without explicit rule provision.

summary.value: The paper introduces NoRA (Non-Path Reasoning with Ambiguous facts), a synthetic benchmark that targets systematic neural relational reasoning beyond the path-composition setting that dominates existing datasets such as CLUTRR and GraphLog. NoRA makes three deliberate design choices: Off-path reasoning, Multi-relational edges, and Cardinality-based ambiguities. Four difficulty metrics (reasoning depth, reasoning width, back-track load (BL) and off-path edge count (OPEC)) are defined and used to build in-distribution training data plus seven out-of-distribution test splits. Extensive experiments with edge-transformers, RAT, several GNNs, NBFNet and two OpenAI LRMs show that all current systems struggle on at least one axis.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Introduces off-path relational reasoning and explicit cardinality ambiguity, two phenomena largely absent from prior synthetic suites such as CLUTRR or GraphLog, thereby filling an important methodological gap.
- Formalizes four orthogonal metrics with precise mathematical definitions and shows how they drive curriculum-style data generation.
- Benchmarks nine graph-reasoning architectures (GNN variants, edge transformers, NBFNet) and two large retrieval-augmented LLMs across in-distribution and seven out-of-distribution splits, uncovering distinct failure modes for each metric.
- Provides the full 284-rule logical ontology, a stochastic story generator, and Croissant-compliant metadata.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- All stories share one family-style ontology and generalization to other domains is untested. Providing at least one additional rule-set to demonstrate portability of the generation pipeline would be helpful.
- Since BL is defined as the maximum number of simultaneous partial bindings the prover must keep alive while exploring a proof tree, in practice it is highly dependent on how individual rules are written. For example, splitting a 3-body rule into two shorter rules may reduces BL from 3 to 1 without changing the underlying reasoning difficulty. A similar drift is observed for OPEC when optional edges are inlined into rules. Consequently, BL/OPEC values cannot be compared across domains unless the rule factorization scheme is fixed.

ethical_comments.value: No significant ethical concerns remain. The benchmark does not involve human subjects, sensitive personal data, or real-world deployment risks.

dataset_code_comments.value: The submission provides both the dataset and code in a readily accessible and well-documented format.

final_justification.value: Overall, while some limitations remain (e.g., full Hetionet results are not yet in the paper), the rebuttal demonstrates that the authors are actively engaging with the concerns raised and expanding their evaluation accordingly. Given the novelty of the evaluation framework, the clear construction of compositional test sets, and the added evidence of generalization potential, I lean toward maintaining my score as Accept. The paper makes a meaningful contribution, particularly in its emphasis on compositional generalization diagnostics for neuro-symbolic reasoning models.

title.value: When No Paths Lead to Rome: Benchmarking Systematic Neural Relational Reasoning

abstract.value: Designing models that can learn to reason in a systematic way is an important and long-standing challenge. In recent years, a wide range of solutions have been proposed for the specific case of systematic relational reasoning, including Neuro-Symbolic approaches, variants of the Transformer architecture, and specialized Graph Neural Networks. However, existing benchmarks for systematic relational reasoning focus on an overly simplified setting, based on the assumption that reasoning can be reduced to composing relational paths. In fact, this assumption is hard-baked into the architecture of several recent models, leading to approaches that can perform well on existing benchmarks but are difficult to generalize to other settings. To support further progress in the field of systematic relational reasoning with neural networks, we introduce a new benchmark that adds several levels of difficulty, requiring models to go beyond path-based reasoning.

venue.value: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track poster

TLDR.value: Reasoning models can learn rules from simple examples and be able to solve complex ones using the rules. We identify a broad class of everyday reasoning rules that current models cannot learn and build large datasets requiring such rule learning.
